scenes.title: Brenda Milner & Henry Molaison ('H.M.'): Day-3 Flawless Mirror-Star Tracing Beside the '30 Errors -> 1 Error' Learning Curve
scenes.era: 1962 / 1968, Hartford & Montreal Neurological Institute testing table

layout.description: Sunlit 1960s neuropsychological testing room with a warm oak desk holding the classic **Mirror-Tracing Apparatus** — an angled metallic hand-occlusion shield hiding direct sight of the paper sheet while an upright framed mirror at the back reflects a crisp **five-pointed double-outline star** and pencil — right beside Brenda Milner's 3-day graph ('Day 1: 30 Errors -> Day 2: 8 Errors -> Day 3: 1 Error | Conscious Recall: 0').

positions.who: Henry Molaison / 'Patient H.M.' (mannequin in neat 1962 buttoned cardigan and collared shirt)
positions.where: sliding his right hand and pencil beneath the metal occlusion shield while watching ONLY the upright mirror — gliding smoothly between the narrow star borders on Day 3 while tilting his head in pleasant surprise ('That looked hard, yet it's so easy!')

positions.who: Brenda Milner (mannequin in 1962 tailored tweed suit jacket and blouse)
positions.where: seated beside the oak desk holding her stopwatch and pointing to the steep 3-day downward error curve

props.name: wooden-and-metal Mirror-Star Tracing Apparatus (occlusion shield + vertical mirror + 5-pointed star sheet)
props.period_detail: blocks direct vision of the hand so only mirror-reversed visual feedback guides the pencil
props.physical_behavior: neuroscience's single most famous tabletop learning device

props.name: Day 1 Jagged Star Sheet vs Day 3 Smooth Star Sheet & 3-Day Error Graph
props.period_detail: contrasts ~30 jagged border crossings on Trial 1 against 1 clean trace on Trial 30
props.physical_behavior: visualizes procedural learning without declarative memory

actions.verb_sequence: places a fresh 5-pointed double-border star sheet under the occlusion shield on Day 3 and asks if Henry has ever tried this -> Henry shakes his head politely ('First time!') -> picks up the pencil and traces all five star points in the mirror smoothly without crossing a border
lifts the shield to inspect his clean star in amused wonder

reactions.reaction: warm, surprised smile at unexpected skill mastery
realizes human memory is NOT one system — founding modern multiple-memory neuroscience

scenes.wardrobe: Early-1960s attire: tailored women's tweed suit and silk blouse; neat men's wool cardigan over white Oxford shirt.
scenes.lighting: Clean high-key New England / Montreal window daylight.
scenes.recognition_hook: On Day 3 he swears politely he has never seen the mirror box in his life — then traces a backwards five-pointed star like an expert on the very first stroke.

key_visual.description: a 1960s neuropsychology desk with a mirror-star tracing apparatus (hand shield, vertical mirror, and five-pointed star sheet) where a seated man traces smoothly beside a 3-day error drop chart

scenes.title: Day 1 Struggle: Fighting Backwards Mirror Physics (30 Errors)
scenes.era: 1962, Day 1 Trial 1 at the testing table

layout.description: Same oak desk showing Trial 1's zigzagging pencil crossings at the tricky star corners.

positions.where: concentrating patiently as the mirror reversal pulls his pencil repeatedly across the star's corners on Trial 1

props.name: Trial-1 star sheet with 30 corner zigzags
props.period_detail: proves the task was genuinely hard at baseline before 3 days of motor learning

actions.verb_sequence: tries moving up-left at a star corner -> mirror reversal zigzags pencil across border -> adjusts steadily

reactions.reaction: counts border crossings calmly on Trial 1

scenes.recognition_hook: Anyone trying a mirror star on Trial 1 zigzags thirty times at the corners — which made Henry's effortless Day-3 glide unmistakable.

scenes.title: Holding '584' for 15 Minutes Until One Knock at the Door

layout.description: Bright quiet testing room with digit cards ('5 — 8 — 4') on the desk.

positions.where: Henry silently rehearsing a 3-digit number flawlessly for 15 minutes via intact prefrontal cortex — until a brief polite knock interrupts rehearsal and the digits vanish

props.name: 3-digit rehearsal card ('584')
props.period_detail: separates intact 20-second prefrontal working memory from missing hippocampal consolidation

actions.verb_sequence: recites '584' accurately after quiet rehearsal -> turns toward door knock -> smiles unable to recall that a number test even happened

reactions.reaction: documents crisp boundary between short-term rehearsal and long-term storage

scenes.wardrobe: Late-1960s collared shirt and lab blazer.
scenes.recognition_hook: Without distractions, intact frontal cortex rehearsed three digits for fifteen straight minutes — one two-second interruption erased the entire test.

scenes.title: Knowing WHAT vs Knowing HOW in Everyday Skill Mastery
scenes.era: Modern sunlit park path / music practice room

layout.description: Sunlit park lane where an adult hops effortlessly onto a bicycle beside a clean two-branch memory map ('Hippocampus: Facts & Events' vs 'Cerebellum/Basal Ganglia: Skills & Habits').

props.name: bicycle & two-branch memory diagram
props.period_detail: connects H.M.'s gift to every human's daily muscle memory

actions.verb_sequence: pushes off smoothly in one balanced motion after years away

scenes.recognition_hook: Every time your fingers find a guitar chord or balance a bicycle after ten years away, you are thanking the procedural brain Henry Molaison revealed to science.
